Seif katan 2, "And slaves." The correct reading is: it is implied by Tur that even those who are not, etc. Tur wrote simply "slaves," whereas in Shulchan Aruch Beit Yosef wrote "freed slaves." Beit Yosef explains that this depends upon how one understands the statement of R' Yehoshua ben Levi that women are obligated in reading the Megillah because "they too were included in that miracle."

According to the explanation that "they too were included in that miracle" means that the miracle itself came about through a woman, unfreed slaves are exempt. Reading the Megillah is a time-bound positive mitzvah, from which women would ordinarily be exempt; their obligation is exceptional because the miracle came through a woman. That rationale does not apply to slaves.

According to the explanation that "they too were included in that miracle" means that women too were included in Haman's decree "to destroy, kill, and annihilate," then the same applies to unfreed slaves. Since they underwent brit milah and immersion and observe the Jewish religion like women, they too were certainly subject, Heaven forbid, to the cup of that decree. Accordingly, they too are obligated.

"And because there are different interpretations." Rashi explains that one divides the length of the sheet into 4 sections: 1 stitching is placed near the top at the end of the first quarter, the second at the midpoint, and the third at the beginning of the lower quarter. Rif explains "in thirds" according to its plain meaning: 2 stitchings are placed at the 2 ends of the sheet and 1 exactly in the middle. Rambam explains "in thirds" to mean 3 stitchings at the top of the sheet, 3 at its bottom, and 3 at its middle. By following the Mechaber's arrangement, one satisfies all of these opinions.

"To give at least," etc. I am uncertain whether a gift to a poor person is effective if given on condition that it be returned. Regarding mishloach manot, such a condition is not effective, because the mitzvah is specifically to give food and drink with which the recipient will rejoice on Purim. If the half-shekel money is distributed to the poor, one fulfills the mitzvah of gifts to the poor through it. [Pri Megadim]

"To 2 poor people." One should not give them the money before Purim, lest they consume it before Purim. [Magen Avraham in the name of HaMaor] The common custom is nevertheless to give money before Purim. Although the mitzvah of gifts to the poor is specifically on Purim day, we must say that people also give 2 gifts to poor people on Purim itself. In addition, there are many poor people who go from door to door on Purim. [Machatzit HaShekel]

"Some say that one should give," etc. It requires study whether a poor person who himself is supported by charity is obligated to give the half-shekel. [Pri Megadim]

"And one should give 3 large halves in these countries." The common interpretation is that "large halves" means 3 half-groschen coins, namely what in our country are called half-groschen. Darkei Moshe does not appear to mean this; see there. Perhaps in his country there was another coin called by that name, because he writes that 1 "large half" equals 9 small peshutim. In our country today that coin does not exist.

According to the currency used in our country, it appears that by strict law one fulfills the practice with the small coin called a half-groschen. Nevertheless, this is not an important coin at all, even if one gives 3 such halves, unless he is also giving on behalf of his minor sons.

I have seen some charity collectors who initially place 3 half-ruble coins into the charity bowl. When a person comes to give the half-shekel, the collector gives him those 3 half-ruble coins in exchange for his money, and the donor then places them into the bowl. This procedure is not satisfactory. If the collector gives them merely as a loan for a few moments and the donor has no intention to transfer ownership of them to charity, then this is not a genuine act of giving at all, and he is merely deceiving himself.

If the collector genuinely intends to transfer ownership to the donor, and the donor then gives them to charity, this is a solution only for the first person, not for those who come afterward. Once the coins have become charity funds, the collector has no authority to exchange them for 3 half-groschen coins. Perhaps, however, because this practice has already become established, it is as though all donors explicitly stipulated that they give the charity under this condition, namely that the collector may use the coins in this manner.

In the time of the Gra, a Polish half-zahuv coin was common. Maaseh Rav records that he would give only 1 Polish half-zahuv. Today that coin is no longer available. One must therefore use either half-groschen coins or a half-ruble coin.

One whom Hashem has blessed with the means to give 1 ruble as a remembrance of the half-shekel, together with 3 half-groschen coins corresponding to the 3 times the word terumah appears in the parashah, in accordance with the latter opinion cited by Rama, is fortunate and it is good for him.

"Seif 1, 'And one who performs,' etc." Pesachim 50b, and similarly wherever there is any trace of transgression.

"And it is permitted to perform any mitzvah-related labor." In the first chapter of Shekalim, on the 15th they read, etc., and repair, etc., even in the walled cities, because it is a mitzvah, as stated there in the Gemara. They prepare it so that if it were not, etc.

"For example, to write." The Mishnah, 17a, states: "He was writing it." Although the Yerushalmi there implies that melacha is permitted, this is because they did not accept Purim as an actual Yom Tov. As a matter of custom, however, melacha may still be restricted, as stated in the Gemara, 5b: "If you wish, say that they always practiced," and regarding Rabbi's planting, etc. This implies that had Purim been an actual Yom Tov, even labor connected to rejoicing would be forbidden.

"And likewise it is permitted." As above regarding planting for rejoicing. The same rationale applies to halachic rulings, as in the verse, "the ordinances," etc.

"Asher Yatzar." See Baer Heitev concerning one who drinks a laxative beverage, etc. Shalmei Tzibbur writes that the widespread custom is to recite Asher Yatzar each time; see there.

However, it appears that where one has severe diarrhea and feels that he will immediately need to relieve himself again, it is forbidden to recite the blessing, as explained below in siman 92, where even Torah study is forbidden under such circumstances; see there. This is also evident from what Shibbolei HaLeket writes in the name of a manuscript responsum of Mahara Nachum. He was asked about one who relieved himself or urinated and did not recite Asher Yatzar: how long does he retain the ability to recite it? He concludes that if he remembers before he again begins to feel the need to relieve himself, he should certainly recite the blessing. If he remembers only after that urge has begun again, he should not recite it. All the more so in the present case.

Regarding what was written concerning one who leaves the restroom, see Eliyah Rabbah, where it is evident from siman 165 that he need not perform an additional washing; see also siman 227.

Nevertheless, some are stringent upon themselves, as written above in siman 4 in the name of Machazik Berachah, that senior rabbis had the practice of washing 3 times after leaving the restroom. See there.

"Because they are close to the bier," etc. Levush explains that this refers specifically to those who are physically close to the bier. Lechem Chamudot, page 19, however, explains Rambam's words differently: in those times, and perhaps still in some places, there were designated groups appointed for carrying the bier. Accordingly, the law applies whether they were presently close to the bier or not. This is also implied by Rambam's commentary on the Mishnah in Perek Mi SheMet.

Nevertheless, in a place where there are no designated groups of bier-bearers, but rather whoever wishes may carry it, Levush's interpretation is correct in practical halacha.

Beit Yosef writes that even though the later groups would have enough time to recite Kriat Shema while the second group is carrying the bier, they are nevertheless exempt, because it can sometimes happen that the third group is called upon to leave in place of the second.

1) [Seif 1] "One is not obligated in tzitzit by Torah law," etc. Meaning a garment of sheep's wool. The same law applies to ram's wool. Beit Yosef; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Eliyah Rabbah, seif katan 1; Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham, letter 1; Machatzit HaShekel, letter 1; Shulchan Gavoah, letter 1; Mor Uketziah; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, siman 9, letter 12. What Baer Heitev writes in seif katan 1 contains a scribal error. I later saw that Maamar Mordechai, letter 5, writes likewise.

2) There, "Or of sheep's wool." Goat hair is called hair, not wool. Camel hair, although it is called camel wool, is not called "wool" without qualification; the same applies to rabbit hair. Beit Yosef; Olat Shabbos; Olat Tamid, letter 2; Machatzit HaShekel there.

3) There, "Or of sheep's wool." If a ewe is the offspring of a goat, its wool is invalid for tzitzit. Rambam, chapter 2. If so, it is not considered wool at all and does not exempt a garment except one of its own type. Beit Yosef; Olat Tamid, letter 2; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham, letter 1. The same applies to a ewe that is the offspring of a ewe that itself is the offspring of a goat; Olat Tamid writes that its status is the same as the direct offspring of a goat. Pri Megadim writes similarly regarding a ewe whose father is a male goat and mother a ewe. Whether these types exempt one another, Pri Megadim leaves requiring study.

4) There, "Or of sheep's wool," etc. If sheep's wool is mixed with other fibers, we follow the majority. Magen Avraham writes that this is also implied by the last chapter of Kilayim. Machatzit HaShekel explains that Magen Avraham means while they are still raw fibers, before threads have been spun from them; at that stage the minority is nullified in the majority, as stated in the Mishnah there and as we rule in Yoreh De'ah, siman 299, seif 1. Once threads have already been spun, however, they are not nullified, as stated there, and so too below in seif katan 4. Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 6, writes likewise.

If the mixture is half and half, Machatzit HaShekel writes that we rule stringently, as stated there in Yoreh De'ah. Meaning, he should use wool tzitzit, which according to the ruling in seif 2 exempts garments of every species. Shulchan Aruch HaRav writes likewise. According to those who hold that wool tzitzit do not exempt garments of other species, as will be explained below with God's help, such a garment would have no solution. Shulchan Aruch HaRav writes this as well.

All this follows Magen Avraham, who holds that even when the materials are of different species we follow the majority in determining the garment's identity. Pri Megadim, however, writes that there is a dispute concerning this, and some hold that nullification by majority applies only where the fibers are of the same species. See there.

5) There, "But garments of other species," etc. {Rama: And some say that all of them are obligated by Torah law, etc.} In the Gemara, Perek HaTekhelet, 39b, there is a dispute whether garments of other materials are obligated in tzitzit by Torah law or only rabbinically. Rav Nachman holds that garments of other species are not Torah-obligated, while Rava holds that they are Torah-obligated as well. Rif and Rambam rule like Rav Nachman, and Maran rules likewise, as is his general method. Tosafot, Rosh, Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and Mordechai rule like Rava, and this is Rama's position.

There is a further dispute in Rava's view. Some hold that even according to Rava, wool or linen tzitzit exempt garments of other materials, and even wool and linen together, despite being kilayim, exempt them. Maharam, however, as cited by Hagahot Maimoniyot, Terumat HaDeshen, and Agur, holds that according to Rava, for other materials that are Torah-obligated, only wool and linen together can exempt them, which applied when tekhelet was available. Nowadays, wool or linen alone do not exempt garments of other materials; each material is exempted only by tzitzit of its own kind, such as silk tzitzit on silk and cotton tzitzit on cotton. This follows the derivation "the corner" means material matching the corner. See Beit Yosef, Bach, and Machatzit HaShekel, seif katan 3.

Therefore every God-fearing person should be stringent for himself and should place cotton tzitzit on a cotton tallis, and similarly with other materials, in order to avoid the dispute. Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 4; Chesed LaAlafim, letter 2; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, siman 9, letter 12; Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Noach, letter 1. See also seif 6 and what we write there.

5) There, "But garments of other species," etc. {Rama: And some say that all of them are obligated by Torah law, etc.} In the Gemara, Perek HaTekhelet, 39b, there is a dispute whether garments of other materials are obligated in tzitzit by Torah law or only rabbinically. Rav Nachman holds that garments of other species are not obligated by Torah law, while Rava holds that garments of other species are likewise Torah-obligated. Rif and Rambam rule like Rav Nachman, and Maran rules likewise, following his usual method. Tosafot, Rosh, Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and Mordechai rule like Rava, and this is Rama's position.

There is also a dispute in Rava's view. Some hold that even according to Rava, wool or linen tzitzit exempt garments of other materials, and even wool and linen together, despite being kilayim, exempt them. Maharam, as cited by Hagahot Maimoniyot, Terumat HaDeshen, and Agur, however, holds that according to Rava, for garments of other materials that are Torah-obligated, only wool and linen together exempt them, which applied when tekhelet was available. Nowadays, wool or linen alone do not exempt garments of other materials; each material is exempted specifically by its own kind, such as silk tzitzit for silk and cotton tzitzit for cotton, because we derive from "the corner" that the tzitzit should be of the material of the corner. See Beit Yosef, Bach, and Machatzit HaShekel, seif katan 3.

Therefore every God-fearing person should be stringent for himself and should place only cotton tzitzit on a cotton tallis, and likewise for other materials, in order to avoid the dispute. Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 4; Chesed LaAlafim, letter 2; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, siman 9, letter 12; Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Noach, letter 1. See seif 6 and our comments there.
Mahari Abuhav and Sefer Mitzvot Katan.
